title: Ser and estar
description: Choose between the two verbs for to be, tell the time, say where things are, and talk about what is going on now.

guide.summary: Portuguese has two verbs for to be. Ser says what something is: identity, nationality, job, character, the time and the date. Estar says how or where something is right now: moods, passing states, where people and things are, and actions in progress with -ndo.

sections.title: Ser: who and what someone is
sections.text: Use ser for what does not change from one moment to the next: who someone is, where they come from, their job and their character. Before a bare profession Portuguese uses no article: Ela é médica.
steps: Ask: is this who or what the person is (name, nationality, job, character)? If so, use ser.
Find the subject and take its row.
Leave out um or uma before a bare profession.
watch: É carries an accent; e without it means and.
A gente (we, informal) takes the ele form: a gente é.

sections.title: Estar: how someone is right now
sections.text: Use estar for states that come and go: moods, feeling tired or ill, being busy or hungry. Words like hoje and agora are a strong clue.
steps: Ask: is this a state that can change by tomorrow? If so, use estar.
Find the subject and take its row.
Write the accents: está and estão.
watch: Está needs its accent: esta without it means this.
Estoy is Spanish; the Portuguese form is spelled with -ou.

sections.title: Telling the time and the date
sections.text: The time, the day and the date take ser, with no subject. From two o'clock on the verb is plural, because horas is plural. Numbers are written as words here.

rows: It is midday. It is midnight.
Hoje é sexta-feira. Hoje é dia dez.
Today is Friday. Today is the tenth.

steps: Use ser, never estar, for the time, the day and the date.
One o'clock, midday or midnight: singular é.
Two o'clock or later: plural são.

examples.en: It is one in the afternoon.

watch: Portuguese has no word for the English it: just São duas horas.
Weather is different: Está frio means it is cold.

sections.title: Saying where something is
sections.text: Where people and movable things are takes estar. For buildings and places Brazilians most often use ficar (O banco fica na praça), or ser; estar is also common: O banco está na praça.
steps: Can the thing move by itself or be picked up? Use estar.
Is it a building, a town or a fixed place? Use ficar (or ser).
Match the verb to a singular or plural subject.
watch: Ser never locates people: As crianças estão na praia, not são.
Ficar with a person means to stay: Eu fico em casa is I stay at home.

sections.title: Same adjective, different meaning
sections.text: Many adjectives work with both verbs. Ser describes what someone or something is like in general; estar describes how it is or seems right now.

rows: Ele é chato: he is a boring person.
Ele está chato: he is being annoying.
Ela é bonita: she is pretty.
Ela está bonita: she looks nice today.
A sopa é boa: it is a good kind of soup.
A sopa está boa: this soup tastes good.
Ele é feliz: he is a happy person.
Ele está feliz: he is happy right now.

steps: Ask whether the sentence is about a lasting trait or the present moment.
Lasting trait: ser. Present moment or a change: estar.
Clues like sempre point to ser; hoje and agora point to estar.
watch: Estar with food or drink is about taste or temperature now: O café está quente.

sections.title: Estar + gerúndio: what is going on now
sections.text: For an action in progress, Brazilians use estar plus the gerúndio, the -ndo form. Drop the final -r of the infinitive and add -ndo.
steps: Put estar in the subject's form.
Take the infinitive and drop the final -r.
Add -ndo: the vowel before it stays a, e or i.
watch: The plain present, Eu leio, means I read in general; for now, say Estou lendo.

steps: Check that the sentence says who or what someone is: nationality, job or character.
Use ser in the subject's form.
No article before a bare profession.
Check that the sentence describes a mood or state that can change.
Use estar in the subject's form, with its accent.
The time, day and date take ser.
One o'clock, midday, midnight: é. Two o'clock and later: são.
People and movable things: estar.
Buildings and fixed places: ficar or ser.
Match singular or plural.
Decide whether the adjective is a lasting trait or how things are now.
Lasting: ser. Now or changed: estar.
Use clues such as sempre, hoje and agora.
Put estar in the subject's form.
Drop the -r of the infinitive and add -ndo.

exercises.hint: Ser is irregular. The eu form is short and ends in -ou.
exercises.feedback: Use the eu form of ser, the verb for who you are.
exercises.explanation: Eu sou: the eu form of ser, as in Eu sou professor.

mistakes.why: That is the eu form of estar, the verb for how you are right now. The verb asked for is ser.
É is the form for você, ele and ela. With eu the verb has its own form.
Somos is the nós form, for a group that includes you. Eu is one person.

exercises.hint: The nós form of almost every verb ends in -mos.
exercises.feedback: Use the nós form of ser.
exercises.explanation: Nós somos: the nós form of ser ends in -mos, like nearly every nós form.

mistakes.why: Estamos is the nós form of estar, the verb for states and places. The verb asked for is ser.
São belongs to vocês, eles and elas. Nós needs its own form ending in -mos.
É is the singular form for você, ele and ela. Nós is a group that includes the speaker.

exercises.hint: The plural form rhymes with não.
exercises.feedback: Use the eles form of ser.
exercises.explanation: Eles são: the form for vocês, eles and elas is the same, and it ends in a nasal -ão.

mistakes.why: Estão is the eles form of estar, used for moods, states and where people are. The verb asked for is ser.
É is singular: one person, você, ele or ela. Eles is several people.
Somos is the nós form and includes the speaker. Eles is a group you are talking about.

exercises.hint: Is nationality a passing state or part of who you are?
exercises.feedback: Nationality describes who someone is.
exercises.explanation: Nationality is identity, so Portuguese uses ser: Eu sou brasileiro.

mistakes.why: Estou comes from estar, the verb for moods and temporary states. Where you are from does not change from day to day.

exercises.instruction: Write ser or estar in the right form.
exercises.hint: A profession says what someone is. Mind the accent.
exercises.feedback: Jobs take ser, and the form for one person you talk about.
exercises.explanation: Profession is identity, so ser: Maria é médica. Note that Portuguese drops the article here: no uma before médica.

mistakes.why: Está comes from estar, for how someone is at the moment. A job is described as part of who a person is.
Without the accent, e means and. The verb needs the acute accent.
São is the plural form. Maria is one person.

exercises.hint: A profession takes ser. Portuguese leaves out the article before a job.
exercises.feedback: Use the nós form of ser and the plural of professor.
exercises.explanation: Nós somos professores: ser for a profession, no article before the job, and the pronoun nós may be dropped because somos already shows the subject.

mistakes.why: Estamos comes from estar, which describes a passing state. A profession is said with the verb of identity.
São is the form for vocês, eles and elas. Nós has its own form ending in -mos.
Portuguese puts no article before a bare profession after ser.

exercises.hint: Being funny is part of her character.
exercises.feedback: Character traits take ser.
exercises.explanation: Minha irmã é muito engraçada: personality is who she is, so ser.

mistakes.why: Está would mean she is being funny right now, today. The English describes her personality.

exercises.hint: What verb names a job?
exercises.feedback: Professions take ser, not estar.
exercises.explanation: Pedro é engenheiro: a profession is identity, so ser, with no article before the job.

mistakes.why: That is the sentence unchanged. Estar is for states and moods; a job is said with the verb of identity.
São is plural. Pedro is one person.
Portuguese leaves out the article before a bare profession.

exercises.hint: The eu form of estar ends in -ou, like the eu form of ser.
exercises.feedback: Use the eu form of estar.
exercises.explanation: Eu estou: est- + -ou. The stress falls on the last syllable.

mistakes.why: That is the eu form of ser, the verb for identity. The verb asked for is estar.
Está is the form for você, ele and ela. Eu has its own form.
Estoy is Spanish. The Portuguese ending is spelled with -ou.

exercises.hint: Você takes the same form as ele and ela. Do not forget the accent.
exercises.feedback: Use the third-person singular form of estar, with its accent.
exercises.explanation: Você está: the accent on the a matters, because without it the word is a different one.

mistakes.why: Without the accent, esta means this (before a feminine noun). The verb needs the acute accent on the last a.
É is the você form of ser, the verb for identity. The verb asked for is estar.
Estou is the eu form. Você is the person you are speaking to.

exercises.hint: Vocês takes the same form as eles and elas.
exercises.feedback: Use the plural form of estar ending in -ão.
exercises.explanation: Vocês estão: the plural form ends in a nasal -ão, like são.

mistakes.why: Estamos is the nós form, which includes the speaker. Vocês is the group you are talking to.
Está is singular. Vocês is several people.
São is the plural form of ser, the verb for identity. The verb asked for is estar.

exercises.hint: Is being tired today a passing state?
exercises.feedback: Tiredness is a state, and hoje says it is about today.
exercises.explanation: Being tired is a temporary state, so estar: Hoje eu estou muito cansado.

mistakes.why: Sou comes from ser, for who you are. Tiredness passes; it is not part of your identity.

exercises.instruction: Write ser or estar in the right form.
exercises.hint: Hunger is a state that passes. The subject is plural.
exercises.feedback: A passing state takes estar, and crianças is plural.
exercises.explanation: Being hungry is a temporary state, and as crianças is plural, so estão.

mistakes.why: São comes from ser, the verb for identity. Hunger is a state that changes during the day.
Está is singular, but crianças is plural.
Estamos is the nós form. The children are people you are talking about.

exercises.hint: Hoje tells you this is about today.
exercises.feedback: A mood that belongs to today takes estar.
exercises.explanation: Eu estou triste hoje: sadness today is a passing mood, so estar.

mistakes.why: That is the sentence unchanged. Ser would make sadness part of who you are, which clashes with hoje.
Está is the form for você, ele and ela. Eu has its own form.
Esta without an accent means this, and it is not the eu form either.

exercises.hint: Being busy is a state of the moment.
exercises.feedback: Use estar with você.
exercises.explanation: Você está ocupado agora? Busy is a passing state, so estar. Use ocupada when asking a woman.

mistakes.why: É comes from ser, which would describe a permanent trait. Busy now is a state of the moment.
Without the accent, esta means this. The verb needs its accent.
Estou is the eu form. Você takes the third-person form.

exercises.hint: Count the hours: one or more than one?
exercises.feedback: Times take ser, plural from two o'clock on.
exercises.explanation: Times use ser, and from two o'clock on the verb is plural because horas is plural: São três horas.

mistakes.why: É is only for one o'clock, midday and midnight. Three hours is plural.
Estar is not used to tell the time. Portuguese uses ser for the hour.

exercises.hint: Days and dates take the same verb as times.
exercises.feedback: Naming the day takes ser.
exercises.explanation: Days of the week and dates take ser: Hoje é sexta-feira.

mistakes.why: Estar is not used to name the day. Portuguese uses ser for days and dates.

exercises.instruction: Write the right form of ser.
exercises.hint: Only one hour. Mind the accent.
exercises.feedback: One o'clock is singular.
exercises.explanation: É uma hora da tarde: one o'clock takes the singular, because uma hora is one hour.

mistakes.why: São is for two o'clock and later. Uma hora is singular.
Estar does not tell the time; the hour is given with ser.
Without the accent, e means and. The verb needs the acute accent.

exercises.hint: Ten hours is plural. There is no word for it.
exercises.feedback: Use the plural of ser and write the number as a word.
exercises.explanation: São dez horas: ser in the plural, because dez horas is more than one hour. Portuguese has no word for the English it.

mistakes.why: É is singular, only for one o'clock, midday and midnight. Ten hours needs the plural verb.
Estar does not tell the time. The hour is given with ser.
Portuguese has no subject for the time. Ele means he.

exercises.hint: Which verb tells the time, and is four hours singular?
exercises.feedback: Times take ser, and quatro horas is plural.
exercises.explanation: São quatro horas: ser for the time, plural from two o'clock on.

mistakes.why: That is the sentence unchanged. Estar does not tell the time.
É is singular, for one o'clock only. Four hours is plural.
Estão is still estar. The time is given with ser.

exercises.instruction: Change the time to two o'clock (duas horas).
exercises.hint: Two hours is plural, so both the verb and hora change.
exercises.feedback: Make the verb and the noun plural.
exercises.explanation: São duas horas: from two o'clock on, ser is plural and hora takes -s.

mistakes.why: É is singular. Two hours is plural, so the verb changes too.
Hora needs the plural -s after duas.
Estar does not tell the time. Keep the verb of the original sentence, just in the plural.

exercises.hint: Keys can be moved from place to place.
exercises.feedback: Things that move take estar for where they are.
exercises.explanation: Keys are movable, so their location takes estar, plural for as chaves: Onde estão as chaves?

mistakes.why: São comes from ser. For things you can pick up and move, Brazilians use estar.

exercises.hint: A bank is a building. It never moves.
exercises.feedback: For fixed places, use ficar (or ser).
exercises.explanation: Buildings and places stay put, so Brazilians locate them with ficar: O banco fica na praça.

mistakes.why: Ficam is plural. O banco is one building.
São is plural, and o banco is one building.

exercises.instruction: Write ser, estar or ficar in the right form.
exercises.hint: Where is a person right now?
exercises.feedback: People are located with estar.
exercises.explanation: A person moves around, so where she is now takes estar: Minha mãe está no trabalho agora.

mistakes.why: Ficar is for fixed places, like buildings. A person changes place during the day.
É comes from ser, which does not locate people.
Without the accent, esta means this. The verb needs its accent.

alternatives.message: Correct and common. Brazilians also say Onde fica o hospital? for buildings.

exercises.hint: A hospital is a fixed building.
exercises.feedback: For a building, use ficar or ser.
exercises.explanation: Onde fica o hospital? Buildings are located with ficar; Onde é o hospital? is just as common.

mistakes.why: Ficam is plural. O hospital is one building.
Estão is plural, and estar is for people and movable things.

exercises.hint: Children move about. Which verb says where people are?
exercises.feedback: People are located with estar.
exercises.explanation: As crianças estão na praia: where people are takes estar, plural for as crianças.

mistakes.why: That is the sentence unchanged. Ser does not say where people are.
Está is singular, but crianças is plural.
Ficam would mean the children stay at the beach. The sentence just says where they are.

answers: Os meus pais estão em casa.
exercises.hint: Parents are people, so which verb places them?
exercises.feedback: People are located with estar.
exercises.explanation: Meus pais estão em casa: estar for where people are, plural for meus pais.

answers: Os meus pais são em casa.
mistakes.why: São comes from ser, which does not say where people are.

exercises.instruction: Change o livro to os livros.
exercises.hint: The subject becomes plural, so the verb does too.
exercises.feedback: Use the plural form of estar.
exercises.explanation: Os livros estão na mesa: books are movable, so estar, and the plural subject takes the plural form.

mistakes.why: Está is singular. Os livros is plural.
São comes from ser. Books you can move are located with estar.
Only the books become plural. There is still one table.

exercises.hint: Is this about soup in general, or the soup you are eating today?
exercises.feedback: Estar with food says how it tastes now.
exercises.explanation: With estar, boa describes how this soup tastes now: A sopa está boa hoje.

mistakes.why: É with boa would describe soup in general, as a kind of food. Hoje points at the soup in front of you.

exercises.source: Meu vizinho ____ chato. Sempre fala muito alto.
exercises.hint: Sempre tells you this is how he always is.
exercises.feedback: A lasting trait takes ser.
exercises.explanation: Sempre shows a lasting trait, so ser: Meu vizinho é chato, he is an annoying person.

mistakes.why: Está would mean he is being annoying right now. Sempre says it is how he always is.

exercises.instruction: Write ser or estar in the right form.
exercises.hint: Hoje makes it about how she looks today.
exercises.feedback: A compliment about today takes estar.
exercises.explanation: Você está muito bonita hoje: estar says how she looks today.

mistakes.why: É would say she is a beautiful person in general. Hoje points at how she looks today.
Without the accent, esta means this. The verb needs its accent.
Estou is the eu form. Você takes the third-person form.

exercises.hint: Is this how he is, or how he is acting today?
exercises.feedback: A personality trait takes ser.
exercises.explanation: Ele é chato: ser makes boring part of who he is.

mistakes.why: Ele está chato means he is being annoying at the moment, not that he is a boring person.
Chata is the feminine form. Ele is a man.

exercises.instruction: Say he is being annoying today, not that he is a boring person. Add hoje at the end.
exercises.hint: A passing mood takes the other verb.
exercises.feedback: Swap ser for estar.
exercises.explanation: Ele está chato hoje: estar makes chato a passing mood, so it means annoying today.

mistakes.why: Ser still makes it his character. A passing mood needs the other verb.
Estou is the eu form. Ele takes the third-person form.
Without the accent, esta means this.

answers: O meu café está frio agora.
exercises.hint: Agora: this is how the coffee is now.
exercises.feedback: How something is at the moment takes estar.
exercises.explanation: Meu café está frio agora: the coffee has gone cold, a changed state, so estar.

mistakes.why: That is the sentence unchanged. Ser would make cold what the coffee is by nature.
Estão is plural. Café is one thing.
Without the accent, esta means this.

exercises.source: Ana is tall and she is tired.
answers: Ana é alta e está cansada.
exercises.hint: One adjective is how she is built, the other how she feels.
exercises.feedback: Height takes ser, tiredness takes estar.
exercises.explanation: Ana é alta e está cansada: height is a lasting trait, ser; tiredness is a passing state, estar.

answers: Ana está alta e é cansada.
mistakes.why: The verbs are swapped. Height lasts; tiredness passes.

exercises.hint: Ongoing actions use estar plus the -ndo form.
exercises.feedback: Estar + gerúndio means doing something right now.
exercises.explanation: Eu estou estudando: estar + gerúndio for what is going on now.

mistakes.why: Ser never combines with the -ndo form. An action in progress is said with estar.

exercises.instruction: Write the gerúndio of the verb.
exercises.hint: -er verbs swap -r for -ndo.
exercises.feedback: Drop -r and add -ndo.
exercises.explanation: Comer becomes comendo: come- + -ndo.

mistakes.why: That is the infinitive. After estar, an action in progress takes the -ndo form.
The vowel stays e for an -er verb: only -ir verbs end in -indo.
Comem is the plain present. After estão the verb takes the -ndo form.

alternatives.message: Eu leio means I read, in general or as a habit. For an action happening now, Brazilians use estar + -ndo.
Leio means I read, in general or as a habit. For an action happening now, Brazilians use estar + -ndo.

exercises.hint: Am reading is an action in progress.
exercises.feedback: Use estar + the -ndo form of ler.
exercises.explanation: Estou lendo um livro: estar + gerúndio. Ler loses its -r and adds -ndo.

mistakes.why: Ser never combines with the -ndo form. An action in progress takes estar.
After estar, an ongoing action takes the -ndo form, not the infinitive.
Ler is an -er verb, so it keeps the e: le- + -ndo.

exercises.instruction: Say it is happening right now: use estar + gerúndio.
exercises.hint: Estar in the ela form, then the -ndo form of cozinhar.
exercises.feedback: -ar verbs swap -r for -ndo.
exercises.explanation: Ela está cozinhando o jantar: está + cozinha- + -ndo.

mistakes.why: Ser never combines with the -ndo form. An action in progress takes estar.
After estar, the verb takes the -ndo form, not the infinitive.
Cozinha is the plain present form. After estar it must end in -ndo.

exercises.instruction: Say it is happening right now: use estar + gerúndio.
exercises.hint: Plural estar, then the -ndo form of dormir.
exercises.feedback: -ir verbs end in -indo.
exercises.explanation: As crianças estão dormindo: estão + dormi- + -ndo.

mistakes.why: Está is singular, but crianças is plural.
Dormir is an -ir verb, so it keeps the i before -ndo.
Ser never combines with the -ndo form.

exercises.source: We are waiting for the bus.
exercises.hint: Esperar takes no word for for.
exercises.feedback: Estar + gerúndio, nós form.
exercises.explanation: Nós estamos esperando o ônibus: estamos + espera- + -ndo. Esperar takes the bus directly, with no preposition.

mistakes.why: Ser never combines with the -ndo form. An action in progress takes estar.

exercises.hint: After estar comes the -ndo form.
exercises.feedback: Estar + gerúndio for an ongoing action.
exercises.explanation: Pedro está estudando português: está + estuda- + -ndo.

mistakes.why: Estudo is the eu present form. After está the verb takes the -ndo form.
That is the infinitive. In Brazil an action in progress is estar + -ndo.
